results.message: Who was Jesus to your world? What did you actually know about him?

voice_event.speaker: ijc
voice_event.text:
To us Jesus is the one our whole argument was about, and the argument itself was our devotion. Our own creed answers first. In substance it says: very God of very God, of one substance with the Father, who for us men and for our salvation came down and was made man; he suffered, and the third day he rose again. A century of councils spent itself making those words exact, because everything hung on them. If the Son is not truly God, then what he gives is not truly God's to give. Leo's own letter, read aloud at Chalcedon, says why the exactness mattered: 'He who is true God is also true man... each form does what is proper to it with the co-operation of the other' - the Word doing what belongs to the Word, the flesh what belongs to the flesh. In the language we actually had, the definitions were the devotion.

What did we actually have about him? Inheritance, not memory. Three hundred years separated these believers from Jesus, and no one alive had met anyone who saw him. What we had was the scriptures, read aloud in every church; the faith each person confessed at baptism; and the creed, which our councils wrote precisely to keep that inheritance from being lost or changed. You can watch us do it. At the council of Chalcedon, when the judges asked the assembly to declare its faith, Rome's legate Paschasinus spoke first and recited the whole chain out loud: the rule of faith set out at Nicaea, confirmed at Constantinople, explained at Ephesus by Cyril, and shown in Leo's own writings. The assembled bishops then cried out their agreement together: so we all believe, so we were baptized, so we baptize. How did we know the resurrection happened? The same way: through the apostles' testimony, carried in scripture and confession, received and tested and held. This world was honest about its own kind of knowing. We guarded the testimony we received. We could not add to it.

results.message: Most people back then couldn't read. How did an ordinary believer ever learn the scriptures?

voice_event.speaker: ijc
voice_event.text:
You ask how someone who could not read ever learned the scriptures, and here is our problem stated plainly. Our record was kept by office-holders - bishops, emperors, courts - and it shows us the channels where scripture moved, not what an ordinary believer experienced receiving it. The channels themselves we can name. Scripture was read aloud in the assembly - every gathering heard it. The newly baptized confessed the creed, which carried the faith in words they spoke themselves. And the psalms were sung, together, which is how scripture became something a person could carry without a page. On one besieged night at Milan the whole congregation sang psalms through the dark, and that enters the record because a bishop and a famous convert both remembered it - but it was the crowd doing the singing, which means they knew the words.

What we cannot show you is one unlettered believer's own account of how the hearing became knowing. That voice does not survive, for this question or any other. We know scripture was read aloud, because councils legislated by it and bishops preached from it, and both acts assume a congregation present to hear. We know the psalms were sung, because Augustine dates exactly when Milan began singing them, and says the practice spread afterward. What the receiving felt like from inside - whether it was enough, whether it left questions, whether anyone struggled to hold it - no one kept those pages. We will not invent them.

citations.sentence: Our record was kept by office-holders - bishops, emperors, courts - and it shows us the channels where scripture moved, not what an ordinary believer experienced receiving it.

results.message: The Bible honestly confuses me sometimes. Did anyone in your world ever struggle with reading it?

voice_event.speaker: ijc
voice_event.text:
We kept one man's struggle with it, and he is not a small witness. Augustine wrote that when he first turned to the Scriptures to see what they were, they seemed lowly to him next to the grand books he was trained on, and he was too proud to stoop. He 'scorned to be a little one,' in his own words. Years later, weeping and asking how long this would take, he heard a child's voice chanting 'take up and read,' and he opened the book at random. 

Here is our limit: that is a famous man's story. What we did not keep is an ordinary reader's struggle. Augustine was a trained public speaker and a bishop, telling his own conversion story long afterwards. A farmer near Hippo who found the reading hard did not leave behind any written record at all. 

We can say this much besides: when our people were afraid, they sang the psalms together. In the dark, scripture became bearable as song.

sources.original_wording: I resolved, therefore, to direct my mind to the Holy Scriptures, that I might see what they were. And behold, I perceive something not comprehended by the proud, not disclosed to children, but lowly as you approach, sublime as you advance, and veiled in mysteries; and I was not of the number of those who could enter into it, or bend my neck to follow its steps. ... Yet, truly, were they such as would develope in little ones; but I scorned to be a little one, and, swollen with pride, I looked upon myself as a great one.
sources.spoken_rendering: So I decided to turn my mind to the Holy Scriptures, to see what they were like. And what I found was something the proud cannot grasp and children are not shown: lowly as you approach it, towering as you go further in, and veiled in mysteries. I was not the kind of person who could enter it, or bow my neck to walk its path. ... The Scriptures were made to help a little one grow; but I scorned to be a little one, and, swollen with pride, I saw myself as a great one.

sources.original_wording: I sent up these sorrowful cries,—'How long, how long? Tomorrow, and tomorrow? Why not now? Why is there not this hour an end to my uncleanness?' I was saying these things and weeping in the most bitter contrition of my heart, when, lo, I heard the voice as of a boy or girl, I know not which, coming from a neighbouring house, chanting, and oft repeating, 'Take up and read; take up and read.' ... So, restraining the torrent of my tears, I rose up, interpreting it no other way than as a command to me from Heaven to open the book, and to read the first Chapter I should light upon.
sources.spoken_rendering: I cried out in sorrow: 'How long, how long? Tomorrow, and tomorrow? Why not now? Why not end my uncleanness this very hour?' I was saying these things and weeping, my heart crushed with bitterness, when I heard a voice from a nearby house (a boy's or a girl's, I could not tell) chanting over and over: 'Take up and read; take up and read.' ... So I held back my flood of tears and stood up. I could take it no other way than as a command from Heaven to open the book and read the first chapter I turned to.
